questions.prompt: Which statement best defines Chemistry at Grade 10 level?
options: The study of matter, its properties and changes
The study of planets and stars only
The study of living organisms only
The study of numbers and shapes
questions.correctAnswer: The study of matter, its properties and changes
questions.explanation: Chemistry focuses on what matter is made of, how it behaves and how it changes during reactions.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the meaning of Chemistry as a field of science.

questions.prompt: Which career is directly supported by knowledge of Chemistry?
questions.explanation: Pharmacists use Chemistry to understand medicines, dosages, reactions and safe handling of substances.
questions.learningOutcome: Explore career opportunities related to Chemistry.

questions.prompt: Which laboratory action best promotes safety when heating a test tube?
options: Point the mouth of the test tube away from people
Look directly into the mouth of the test tube
Hold the test tube with bare fingers
Fill the test tube completely before heating
questions.correctAnswer: Point the mouth of the test tube away from people
questions.explanation: Pointing the mouth away reduces injury risk if hot liquid or vapour splashes out.
questions.learningOutcome: Promote rights and responsibilities in a safe learning environment.

questions.prompt: Which information on a medicine label helps prevent overdose?
questions.explanation: Dosage instructions state how much medicine should be taken and how often it should be used.
questions.learningOutcome: Examine safe use of drugs and substances in day to day life.

questions.prompt: Which example shows Chemistry helping agriculture in Kenya?
options: Testing soil acidity before applying lime
Counting the number of trees in a farm
Measuring the length of a fence
Choosing the colour of a school uniform
questions.correctAnswer: Testing soil acidity before applying lime
questions.explanation: Soil acidity and liming involve chemical ideas about acids, bases and soil nutrients.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate Chemistry to day to day activities and local industries.

questions.prompt: Which subatomic particle has a positive charge?
questions.explanation: A proton is positively charged, an electron is negatively charged and a neutron has no charge.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the structure of the atom.

questions.prompt: Where are protons and neutrons found in an atom?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, while electrons occupy energy levels around it.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the structure of the atom.

questions.prompt: What does the atomic number of an element show?
questions.explanation: Atomic number is defined by the number of protons in the nucleus of each atom of an element.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate atomic number to atomic structure.

questions.prompt: Which pair represents isotopes of the same element?
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different mass numbers because their neutron numbers differ.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the meaning of isotopes.

questions.prompt: Which notation represents the electron arrangement of sodium using shells?
questions.explanation: Sodium has 11 electrons, arranged as 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 1 in the third.
questions.learningOutcome: Write electron arrangements for the first 20 elements.

questions.prompt: Which element is in Group 1 and Period 3 of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Sodium has one outer electron and three occupied shells, so it is in Group 1 and Period 3.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate the position of an element to its electron arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which family of elements is found in Group VII of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Group VII contains halogens such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify chemical families using the periodic table.

questions.prompt: What type of ion is formed when an atom loses electrons?
questions.explanation: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion has a positive charge.
questions.learningOutcome: Illustrate ion formation of elements.

questions.prompt: Which type of chemical bond is formed by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal?
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding forms when electrons are transferred and oppositely charged ions attract each other.
questions.learningOutcome: Illustrate bond types in elements and compounds.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes a covalent bond?
options: A shared pair of electrons between atoms
An attraction between metal layers only
A mixture of ions in water
questions.correctAnswer: A shared pair of electrons between atoms
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding involves atoms sharing pairs of electrons to gain stable outer energy levels.
questions.learningOutcome: Illustrate bond types in molecules and compounds.

questions.prompt: A medicine label says take two tablets after meals. Which responsible action follows chemical safety ideas?
options: Take only the stated dose and seek advice if unsure
Take more tablets to recover faster
Ignore the expiry date if the colour looks normal
questions.correctAnswer: Take only the stated dose and seek advice if unsure
questions.explanation: Safe use of medicines depends on following dosage instructions, expiry dates and professional advice.
questions.learningOutcome: Examine safe use of drugs and substances in day to day life.

questions.prompt: Which branch of Chemistry is most concerned with carbon compounds such as fuels and plastics?
questions.explanation: Organic chemistry studies most carbon compounds, including many fuels, plastics and natural products.
questions.learningOutcome: Discuss branches of Chemistry and their applications.

questions.prompt: Which pair of particles determines the mass number of an atom?
questions.explanation: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate mass number to the structure of the atom.

questions.prompt: An atom has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Neutrons are found by subtracting atomic number from mass number: 24 minus 12 equals 12.
questions.learningOutcome: Determine numbers of subatomic particles in atoms.

questions.prompt: Which electron arrangement belongs to calcium, atomic number 20?
questions.explanation: Calcium has 20 electrons, arranged in shells as 2, 8, 8 and 2.
questions.learningOutcome: Write electron arrangements for the first 20 elements.

questions.prompt: Which electron configuration in s and p notation represents neon?
questions.explanation: Neon has 10 electrons, filling 1s, 2s and 2p orbitals as 1s2 2s2 2p6.
questions.learningOutcome: Write electron arrangement using s and p notation.

questions.prompt: Chlorine has two common isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. What is different between them?
questions.explanation: Isotopes of chlorine have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain isotopes using atomic structure.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion came from Rutherford's gold foil experiment?
options: Most of the atom is empty space with a small dense nucleus
Electrons are found inside the nucleus
questions.correctAnswer: Most of the atom is empty space with a small dense nucleus
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed through the foil, while a few were deflected by a small dense positive nucleus.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe evidence for the nuclear model of the atom.

questions.prompt: Which element has the shell arrangement 2,8,7?
questions.explanation: The arrangement 2,8,7 contains 17 electrons, which is the atomic number of chlorine.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate electron arrangement to element identity.

questions.prompt: Why are noble gases generally unreactive?
options: They have stable outer electron arrangements
They are all liquids at room temperature
questions.correctAnswer: They have stable outer electron arrangements
questions.explanation: Noble gases already have stable outer shells, so they have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate stability of atoms to electron arrangement.

questions.prompt: A magnesium atom forms Mg2+. What has happened to its electrons?
questions.explanation: Magnesium has two outer electrons and forms Mg2+ by losing both to reach a stable arrangement.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict ion formation from electron arrangement.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of aluminium oxide given Al3+ and O2- ions?
questions.explanation: Two Al3+ ions give a total charge of +6, balancing three O2- ions with a total charge of -6.
questions.learningOutcome: Derive formulae of compounds from ion charges.

questions.prompt: Which equation is balanced for magnesium reacting with oxygen?
questions.explanation: The equation has two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms on both sides.
questions.learningOutcome: Write balanced equations for simple reactions.

questions.prompt: Which substance is likely to have giant ionic structure?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride consists of many Na+ and Cl- ions arranged in a giant ionic lattice.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate bond types to structures of substances.

questions.prompt: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: Its ions are free to move
questions.correctAnswer: Its ions are free to move
questions.explanation: In molten sodium chloride, ions can move through the liquid and carry electric charge.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate the relationship between bond type and electrical conductivity.

questions.prompt: Which property is typical of simple covalent molecules such as methane?
questions.explanation: Simple covalent molecules have weak forces between molecules, so less energy is needed to separate them.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate bond types to physical properties of substances.

questions.prompt: Which bonding model best explains why aluminium conducts electricity as a solid?
options: Metal ions in a lattice with delocalised electrons
Neutral molecules held by weak forces
Positive and negative ions fixed with no mobile charge
Single atoms not touching one another
questions.correctAnswer: Metal ions in a lattice with delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Metals conduct because delocalised electrons move through the metallic lattice.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate metallic bonding to physical properties.

questions.prompt: Which trend occurs down Group I from lithium to potassium?
options: Outer electrons become more strongly held
questions.explanation: Down Group I, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily, increasing reactivity.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe trends in properties of Group I elements.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes halogen reactivity down Group VII?
questions.explanation: Halogens become less reactive down the group because gaining an electron becomes harder as atomic size increases.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe trends in properties of Group VII elements.

questions.prompt: Which observation is expected when sodium reacts with cold water?
options: Oxygen gas relights a glowing splint
questions.explanation: Sodium reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, producing fizzing.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate chemical properties of Group I elements.

questions.prompt: What is the colour of chlorine gas under ordinary laboratory conditions?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas and should only be handled with strict safety precautions.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe physical properties of Group VII elements.

questions.prompt: Which ion is mainly responsible for acidic behaviour in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: Acids produce hydrogen ions in aqueous solution, which give acids their characteristic behaviour.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain characteristics of acids in aqueous solutions.

questions.prompt: Which ion is mainly responsible for alkaline behaviour in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: Alkalis produce hydroxide ions in water, giving them alkaline properties.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain characteristics of bases in aqueous solutions.

questions.prompt: What gas is usually produced when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
questions.explanation: Acids react with carbonates to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe chemical properties of acids.

questions.prompt: Which pH value is strongly acidic?
questions.explanation: On the pH scale, lower values are more acidic, while values above 7 are alkaline.
questions.learningOutcome: Use the pH scale to classify solutions.

questions.prompt: A school wants to test whether bottled water is acidic, neutral or alkaline. Which material is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Universal indicator shows a range of colours that can estimate pH and classify the solution.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify acids and bases using universal indicator.

questions.prompt: Which substance is a weak acid commonly found in vinegar?
questions.explanation: Vinegar contains ethanoic acid, which only partially ionises in water.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify acids as strong or weak in aqueous solution.

questions.prompt: Which salt is a normal salt formed from complete neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Complete neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide forms sodium chloride and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify salts based on their properties.

questions.prompt: Which method is best for preparing insoluble barium sulphate in the laboratory?
options: Precipitation using two soluble salt solutions
Direct reaction of sodium with water
questions.correctAnswer: Precipitation using two soluble salt solutions
questions.explanation: Insoluble salts such as barium sulphate are prepared by mixing suitable soluble solutions to form a precipitate.
questions.learningOutcome: Prepare salts using appropriate laboratory methods.

questions.prompt: Which salt is deliquescent?
questions.explanation: Deliquescent substances absorb water vapour from air until they dissolve in the absorbed water.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the behaviour of salts when exposed to air.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes efflorescence in hydrated salts?
options: Loss of water of crystallisation to the air
Absorption of water until a solution forms
Reaction with oxygen to form an oxide
Change from solid directly to gas
questions.correctAnswer: Loss of water of crystallisation to the air
questions.explanation: Efflorescent salts lose some or all of their water of crystallisation when exposed to air.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the behaviour of salts when exposed to air.

questions.prompt: Which group of salts is generally soluble in water?
questions.explanation: Nitrates are generally soluble, while many carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble except those of some Group I ions and ammonium.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify salts as soluble or insoluble.

questions.prompt: Which use of salts is linked to agriculture?
questions.explanation: Some salts provide plant nutrients, but they must be used carefully to reduce environmental harm.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline applications of salts in day to day life.

questions.prompt: Which statement explains why excessive fertiliser use can cause eutrophication?
options: Nutrients wash into water bodies and encourage rapid algal growth
Fertilisers turn all water into strong acid instantly
Fertilisers remove all dissolved oxygen directly
Fertilisers stop all plant growth in soil
questions.correctAnswer: Nutrients wash into water bodies and encourage rapid algal growth
questions.explanation: Runoff carrying nitrates and phosphates can cause algal blooms that later reduce oxygen in water.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate effects of salt applications on environmental sustainability.

questions.prompt: Which formula represents methane, the simplest alkane?
questions.explanation: Methane has one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms and is the simplest alkane.
questions.learningOutcome: Recognise simple organic compounds and their formulae.

questions.prompt: Why can carbon form many different organic compounds?
options: Each carbon atom can form four covalent bonds
Carbon is always an ion in compounds
Carbon cannot bond to other carbon atoms
questions.correctAnswer: Each carbon atom can form four covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Carbon is tetravalent and can bond to carbon and many other elements in different structures.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain carbon bonding in simple organic compounds.

questions.prompt: Which general formula represents alkanes?
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons and follow the general formula CnH2n+2.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify simple homologous series using general formulae.

questions.prompt: Which substance is an organic compound?
questions.explanation: Ethanol is a carbon compound with C-H bonds, so it is classified as an organic compound.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify simple substances as organic or inorganic.

questions.prompt: A hydrocarbon contains only which elements?
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
questions.learningOutcome: Recognise simple hydrocarbons by composition.

questions.prompt: The isotopes of boron are boron-10 at 20% abundance and boron-11 at 80% abundance. What is the relative atomic mass?
questions.explanation: The weighted average is (10 x 20 + 11 x 80) divided by 100, giving 10.8.
questions.learningOutcome: Determine relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances.

questions.prompt: Which electron configuration represents magnesium in s and p notation?
questions.explanation: Magnesium has 12 electrons, filling up to 3s2 after the neon core.
questions.learningOutcome: Write electron arrangement using s and p notation for first 20 elements.

questions.prompt: Which atom has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 13 electrons?
questions.explanation: The atomic number 13 identifies aluminium, and 13 protons plus 14 neutrons gives mass number 27.
questions.learningOutcome: Use subatomic particles to identify atoms and mass numbers.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares atoms and ions?
options: Atoms are neutral, while ions carry a charge
Atoms always have more electrons than protons
Atoms are made only from neutrons
questions.correctAnswer: Atoms are neutral, while ions carry a charge
questions.explanation: Atoms have equal numbers of protons and electrons, while ions form when electrons are lost or gained.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain ion formation from electron gain or loss.

questions.prompt: Which ion is formed by an oxygen atom with electron arrangement 2,6?
questions.explanation: Oxygen gains two electrons to complete its outer shell, forming an oxide ion with a 2- charge.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict type of ion formed from electron arrangement.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of calcium nitrate, given Ca2+ and NO3- ions?
questions.explanation: One Ca2+ ion needs two nitrate ions, each with a 1- charge, to make a neutral compound.
questions.learningOutcome: Derive formulae of compounds using valencies and radicals.

questions.prompt: Which equation is balanced for sodium reacting with chlorine?
questions.explanation: Two sodium atoms react with one chlorine molecule to form two formula units of sodium chloride.
questions.learningOutcome: Write balanced equations for simple reactions.

questions.prompt: In ammonium ion, NH4+, how is the fourth N-H bond commonly described?
questions.explanation: The nitrogen atom donates a lone pair to H+, forming a dative covalent bond in NH4+.
questions.learningOutcome: Illustrate dative covalent bonding in selected ions.

questions.prompt: Which force mainly explains the unusually high boiling point of water compared with similar small molecules?
questions.explanation: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than ordinary Van der Waals forces between small molecules.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate intermolecular forces to physical properties.

questions.prompt: Why is graphite able to conduct electricity?
options: It has delocalised electrons between carbon layers
questions.correctAnswer: It has delocalised electrons between carbon layers
questions.explanation: In graphite, each carbon bonds to three others, leaving electrons that can move along the layers.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate structure and bonding to uses of substances.

questions.prompt: Which structure explains why diamond is very hard?
options: A giant covalent network with strong bonds throughout
Layers held by only weak forces
questions.correctAnswer: A giant covalent network with strong bonds throughout
questions.explanation: Diamond has each carbon atom covalently bonded to four others in a strong three-dimensional network.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate bond type and structure to physical properties.

questions.prompt: Across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine, what generally happens to atomic radius?
options: It changes randomly with no pattern
questions.explanation: Nuclear charge increases across the period while electrons enter the same main shell, pulling atoms smaller.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe trends in physical properties across a period.

questions.prompt: Which Period 3 element is a noble gas?
questions.explanation: Argon is in Group VIII and has a stable full outer electron arrangement.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify chemical families and their properties.

questions.prompt: Chlorine is added to potassium bromide solution. Which observation is expected?
options: The solution turns orange-brown as bromine forms
A white precipitate of sodium chloride forms
Hydrogen gas burns with a pop
The solution becomes colourless because potassium forms
questions.correctAnswer: The solution turns orange-brown as bromine forms
questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and displaces bromide ions to form bromine.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate displacement reactions of halogens.

questions.prompt: Which test confirms hydrogen gas produced when a reactive metal reacts with dilute acid?
options: A burning splint gives a pop sound
Damp blue litmus turns red then bleaches
questions.correctAnswer: A burning splint gives a pop sound
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns rapidly with oxygen, producing a characteristic pop sound.
questions.learningOutcome: Collect and test gases produced in reactions of metals.

questions.prompt: Which acid-base reaction is neutralisation?
questions.explanation: Neutralisation is a reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe chemical properties of acids and bases.

questions.prompt: Two solutions have the same concentration. Hydrochloric acid conducts electricity better than ethanoic acid. Why?
options: Hydrochloric acid ionises more completely in water
Hydrochloric acid is a solid metal
Ethanoic acid contains no hydrogen atoms
questions.correctAnswer: Hydrochloric acid ionises more completely in water
questions.explanation: A strong acid produces more mobile ions than a weak acid of the same concentration, so it conducts better.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare electrical conductivity of strong and weak acids.

questions.prompt: Which oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and bases.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate oxides and hydroxides that react with both acids and bases.

questions.prompt: A student wants dry crystals of copper(II) sulphate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulphuric(VI) acid. Which step removes excess copper(II) oxide?
questions.explanation: Excess insoluble copper(II) oxide is removed by filtration before concentrating the filtrate to crystallise the salt.
questions.learningOutcome: Prepare salts using appropriate laboratory methods.

questions.prompt: Which ionic equation represents precipitation of silver chloride?
questions.explanation: Silver ions and chloride ions combine to form insoluble silver chloride precipitate.
questions.learningOutcome: Write ionic equations for precipitation reactions.

questions.prompt: Which drying agent works well because it is hygroscopic but should not react with the gas being dried?
questions.explanation: Anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs moisture and is used when it does not chemically react with the gas.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply behaviour of salts in air to laboratory use.

questions.prompt: Which method is most suitable for preparing sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
options: Heating sodium metal in chlorine in an open classroom
questions.explanation: Both reactants are soluble, so titration finds the neutral point before evaporation gives the salt crystals.
questions.learningOutcome: Choose appropriate methods for preparing soluble salts.

questions.prompt: Which practical step reduces environmental harm after preparing salts in a school laboratory?
options: Dispose of waste as instructed instead of pouring all chemicals into drains
Mix all leftover chemicals to save space
Leave residues on benches to dry
Throw labelled solutions into ordinary paper bins
questions.correctAnswer: Dispose of waste as instructed instead of pouring all chemicals into drains
questions.explanation: Safe disposal prevents avoidable pollution, corrosion and harmful reactions in drainage systems.
questions.learningOutcome: Promote safe waste management during salt preparation.

questions.prompt: Which option best explains why sodium chloride has a high melting point?
options: Strong electrostatic attraction between many oppositely charged ions
Weak forces between separate neutral molecules
Only one covalent bond in each crystal
Free electrons boiling at room temperature
questions.correctAnswer: Strong electrostatic attraction between many oppositely charged ions
questions.explanation: A giant ionic lattice needs much energy to overcome attractions between many positive and negative ions.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate ionic bonding and structure to melting point.

questions.prompt: Why is graphite used as a lubricant while diamond is not?
options: Graphite has layers that slide over each other
Graphite has stronger bonds in all directions than diamond
Diamond is made of ions that slide easily
Diamond dissolves in oil to reduce friction
questions.correctAnswer: Graphite has layers that slide over each other
questions.explanation: Weak forces between graphite layers allow the layers to slide, making graphite useful as a lubricant.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate resultant structures to uses of substances.

questions.prompt: A substance conducts electricity as a solid and can be hammered into sheets. Which bonding type is most likely?
questions.explanation: Metals conduct as solids and are malleable because metal layers can slide while delocalised electrons remain mobile.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate metallic bonding to conductivity and malleability.

questions.prompt: Which prediction is valid for an element with electron arrangement 2,8,8,1?
options: It forms a +1 ion and belongs to Group I
It forms a -1 ion and belongs to Group VII
It is a noble gas in Group VIII
It forms a +2 ion and belongs to Group II
questions.correctAnswer: It forms a +1 ion and belongs to Group I
questions.explanation: One outer electron indicates Group I behaviour and loss of that electron forms a +1 ion.
questions.learningOutcome: Infer valency and ion formation from electron arrangement.

questions.prompt: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in SO4 2-?
questions.explanation: Four oxygen atoms contribute -8 in total, so sulphur must be +6 to give the ion an overall 2- charge.
questions.learningOutcome: Infer oxidation numbers in radicals and compounds.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of ammonium sulphate given NH4+ and SO4 2-?
questions.explanation: Two ammonium ions, each with a 1+ charge, balance one sulphate ion with a 2- charge.
questions.learningOutcome: Derive formulae using radicals and ion charges.

questions.prompt: Which balanced equation represents calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: A carbonate reacts with an acid to produce a salt, carbon dioxide and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Write balanced equations for reactions of acids with carbonates.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best links Group I reactivity to atomic structure?
options: Outer electrons are lost more easily as atomic radius increases down the group
Atoms gain protons as they go down the group
All Group I atoms have full outer shells
Nuclear charge becomes zero down the group
questions.correctAnswer: Outer electrons are lost more easily as atomic radius increases down the group
questions.explanation: More inner shells shield the outer electron, so it is less strongly attracted and is lost more readily.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain trends in chemical properties of Group I elements.

questions.prompt: Why does chlorine displace iodine from potassium iodide solution?
options: Chlorine is more reactive and gains electrons more readily than iodine
Iodine is a metal and chlorine is not
Potassium reacts faster with iodine than chlorine
Chlorine has a higher mass number than iodine
questions.correctAnswer: Chlorine is more reactive and gains electrons more readily than iodine
questions.explanation: A more reactive halogen displaces the halide ion of a less reactive halogen from solution.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain chemical reactions of Group VII elements.

questions.prompt: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across Period 3?
options: Nuclear charge increases while shielding changes little
Atoms gain extra inner shells across the period
Outer electrons move farther from the nucleus every step
questions.correctAnswer: Nuclear charge increases while shielding changes little
questions.explanation: The stronger attraction between nucleus and outer electrons generally makes electron removal harder across the period.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe trends in ionisation energy across a period.

questions.prompt: Which safety reason best explains why chlorine gas preparation must be done in a fume cupboard or well controlled setup?
options: Chlorine is toxic and irritates the respiratory system
Chlorine is a harmless food gas
Chlorine is always solid at room temperature
Chlorine cannot react with any substance
questions.correctAnswer: Chlorine is toxic and irritates the respiratory system
questions.explanation: Chlorine gas is harmful when inhaled, so learners must avoid direct exposure and follow laboratory safety rules.
questions.learningOutcome: Observe safety while investigating properties of chlorine.

questions.prompt: A salt sample absorbs moisture from air but does not dissolve in that moisture. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: A hygroscopic substance absorbs moisture without necessarily dissolving to form a solution.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify salts by their behaviour in air.

questions.prompt: A farmer near Lake Victoria wants to reduce nutrient runoff from inorganic fertilisers. Which practice is most responsible?
options: Apply recommended amounts and avoid spreading fertiliser before heavy rain
Double the fertiliser to reduce weeds
Apply fertiliser directly into drainage channels
Wash unused fertiliser into a stream
questions.correctAnswer: Apply recommended amounts and avoid spreading fertiliser before heavy rain
questions.explanation: Using the recommended amount at the right time reduces nutrient loss to water bodies and protects ecosystems.
questions.learningOutcome: Suggest mitigation measures for environmental effects of salts.

questions.prompt: A learner designs an investigation to compare strong and weak acids of the same concentration. Which plan gives the best evidence?
options: Measure pH and electrical conductivity for equal volumes of each acid
Compare only the smell of each acid
Use different concentrations and record colour only
Heat each acid until it evaporates completely
questions.correctAnswer: Measure pH and electrical conductivity for equal volumes of each acid
questions.explanation: pH and conductivity show the extent of ionisation when concentration and volume are controlled.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a fair comparison of strong and weak acids.

questions.prompt: A colourless solution turns universal indicator purple. Which conclusion and next safety action are best?
options: It is strongly alkaline, so handle it with eye protection and avoid skin contact
It is neutral, so taste it to confirm
It is weakly acidic, so pour it on the bench
It is pure water, so store it in a drink bottle
questions.correctAnswer: It is strongly alkaline, so handle it with eye protection and avoid skin contact
questions.explanation: Purple universal indicator shows strong alkalinity, and strong alkalis are corrosive enough to need careful handling.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret indicator results and apply laboratory safety.

questions.prompt: A student must prepare pure dry lead(II) sulphate. Which sequence is most appropriate?
options: Mix soluble lead(II) nitrate and sodium sulphate, filter, wash and dry the precipitate
React lead metal with dilute sulphuric(VI) acid and evaporate to dryness
Mix sand with water, filter and keep the filtrate
Heat lead(II) sulphate until it melts and pour it into water
questions.correctAnswer: Mix soluble lead(II) nitrate and sodium sulphate, filter, wash and dry the precipitate
questions.explanation: Lead(II) sulphate is insoluble, so precipitation followed by filtration, washing and drying gives a pure solid.
questions.learningOutcome: Select an appropriate laboratory method for preparing an insoluble salt.

questions.prompt: A student finds a white salt becomes powdery after standing in air. Which explanation best fits this observation?
options: It is efflorescent and loses water of crystallisation
It is deliquescent and forms a solution
It is a metal that rusts instantly
It is an acid reacting with oxygen
questions.correctAnswer: It is efflorescent and loses water of crystallisation
questions.explanation: Efflorescent hydrated salts lose water to the atmosphere, often leaving a powdery surface.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse observations of salts exposed to air.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for sodium chloride dissolving in water but not conducting as a solid?
options: Water separates ions so they move, but solid ions are fixed in the lattice
Water creates electrons from sodium atoms only
Solid sodium chloride has no charged particles
Solid sodium chloride contains only covalent molecules
questions.correctAnswer: Water separates ions so they move, but solid ions are fixed in the lattice
questions.explanation: Ions carry current only when mobile, as in molten or aqueous sodium chloride.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse how bonding and structure affect solubility and conductivity.

questions.prompt: Which model would best show ionic bonding in magnesium oxide for a class project?
options: Magnesium losing two electrons to oxygen, forming Mg2+ and O2- ions in a lattice
Magnesium and oxygen sharing one pair of electrons equally
Separate Mg and O atoms floating without attraction
questions.correctAnswer: Magnesium losing two electrons to oxygen, forming Mg2+ and O2- ions in a lattice
questions.explanation: Magnesium oxide is ionic because magnesium transfers two electrons to oxygen and the resulting ions attract.
questions.learningOutcome: Model bonding in selected compounds using electron transfer.

questions.prompt: An unknown Period 3 element forms an oxide that reacts with both acids and alkalis. Which element is most likely?
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, unlike the strongly basic oxide of sodium or acidic oxides of many non-metals.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse trends in Period 3 oxides and their reactions.

questions.prompt: Which set of observations best supports the trend that halogens become less reactive down Group VII?
options: Chlorine displaces bromide and iodide, while iodine does not displace chloride
Iodine displaces chlorine from chloride solution
All halogens displace each other equally
Bromine changes into sodium in solution
questions.correctAnswer: Chlorine displaces bromide and iodide, while iodine does not displace chloride
questions.explanation: A more reactive halogen displaces ions of less reactive halogens, showing chlorine is more reactive than iodine.
questions.learningOutcome: Use displacement evidence to analyse Group VII reactivity trends.

questions.prompt: Magnesium has isotopes 24Mg at 79%, 25Mg at 10% and 26Mg at 11%. What is its relative atomic mass to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The weighted average is 24(0.79) + 25(0.10) + 26(0.11), which equals 24.32.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate relative atomic mass from several isotopic abundances.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to classify an unknown solid as ionic, simple molecular, metallic or giant covalent. Which test set is most useful?
options: Melting point, solubility, and electrical conductivity as solid, molten and aqueous forms
Colour only and whether it has a smell
Mass only and the brand of its container
How loudly it sounds when tapped once
questions.correctAnswer: Melting point, solubility, and electrical conductivity as solid, molten and aqueous forms
questions.explanation: Those tests connect directly to particle arrangement, bonding and mobility of charged particles.
questions.learningOutcome: Design investigations linking bond type to physical properties.
